newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Albright tour of guerrilla camp marks new era.
newsitem.headline: Albright tour of guerrilla camp marks new era.

text.p: Guatemala's bitter guerrilla war and the murky U.S. role in it were consigned to the past on Sunday as U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright toured a demobilization camp for former insurgents.
Smiles and handshakes replaced anti-American slogans as U.S. officials said the Cold War was finally over with the formal end of Central America's last guerrilla conflict.
The ex-rebels proclaimed that they would fight on -- but only politically.

Albright was visiting Guatemala to celebrate the success of the country's peace process, which has seen thousands of guerrillas turn in their assault rifles and start civilian lives under an agreement signed last December.

Demobilization was declared complete last Friday, and seven of eight camps where the fighters disarmed were closed. This one, at Tululche in northwest Guatemala, remained open as a half-way house for those who have not yet resettled.
"This is the end of the Cold War," remarked a senior U.S. official accompanying Albright. "These are the last warriors."

Guerrilla insurgencies continue in Colombia and Peru, but the 36-year war in Guatemala was a classic Cold War conflict, with the United States funding and training the forces of rightist military regimes against leftist guerrillas.
The aid was cut off in 1990 after the U.S. Congress began looking into the Guatemalan army's human rights abuses.

There was little talk of the one-time American role as Albright, dressed in khaki shirt and trousers and sporting a straw hat, arrived in a cloud of dust aboard a U.S. military Blackhawk helicopter at the camp set in a jungle clearing.

Everywhere she went, hand-written posters of the Guatemalan Revolutionary National Unit (URNG) were plastered on buildings, proclaiming that the guerrillas had not surrendered and would carry on their fight by other means.
"We will continue struggling for real democracy with social justice," said one Spanish-language poster. "We swear to win and never surrender," read another.

But there was an enthusiastic welcome for Albright as about 200 local villagers, mainly women and children, joined the handful of former fighters still living at the camp, a collection of plywood cabins with corrugated metal roofs.

Albright was shown around by a guerrilla leader dubbed Comandante Randal, his combat dress replaced by shirt and jeans. She distributed colouring books as presents for the children and apologised that she did not have enough.

Speaking to U.N. officials and soldiers who supervised the demobilization, Albright hailed the partially U.S.-funded peace process. "These amazing peace accords have provided a blueprint for the way Guatemalans ought to live," she said.
Later, she told the assembled throng that this was "a wonderful celebration" and they now had "a chance to live in peace and happiness".

"Some of you may wonder what in heaven's sake is the Secretary of State of the United States doing here," she said. "The reason is because we are all one family, and when one part of the family suffers, we all suffer."
Applause greeted her remarks, although officials said many of the villagers spoke only Indian languages and would not understand even the Spanish interpretation.
A former guerrilla, Baltazar Zapeta, alias Comandante Hernan, told reporters he viewed the prospect of peace "with a kind of optimism".

"Now with these peace accords, there's no need to fight with guns any more. We're going to strengthen our political battle. We have a strong social and political base and we're going to consolidate this."
